title: Design a distributed message queue (Kafka-like)
scopeHtml: Scope: partitioned log, replication and ISR, producers and consumer groups, delivery semantics, retention.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
A distributed message queue lets producers write messages that consumers read later, decoupling the two. A Kafka-like system is a durable, partitioned, replicated log. LinkedIn built Kafka to move activity events; now Uber, Netflix and most big companies use it as the backbone between services.

Functional

  • Producers publish messages to a topic.
  • Consumers subscribe and read messages; consumer groups share the work.
  • Messages keep their order within a partition; replay from any offset.
  • Retention: keep messages for N days (not deleted on read).

Non-functional

  • Throughput: millions of messages/s across the cluster.
  • Durability: acknowledged messages survive broker failures.
  • Availability: brokers can fail without stopping producers/consumers.
  • Low latency (single-digit ms to tens of ms end to end).
  • Scale by adding brokers and partitions.

Decision gravity. Choosing a log (append-only, offset-based, retained) over a classic queue (delete after ack, as RabbitMQ/SQS) is the root decision: it allows replay and many independent readers, but gives up per-message ack/redelivery and priority. Reversible only at high migration cost; consumers depend on offset semantics.

Everyday analogy. A newspaper archive: publishers add editions to the end; each reader keeps a bookmark and can reread old ones.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating Kafka like RabbitMQ (per-message delete, priorities).
  • Forgetting replay and multiple consumer groups as requirements.
  • Not asking about ordering guarantees.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
Producer

POST /v1/topics/orders/messages        (or client library send())
{ "key": "user-42", "value": "<bytes>", "headers": {"traceId":"abc"},
  "acks": "all", "idempotentProducerId": 7712, "sequence": 1034 }

200 { "partition": 3, "offset": 889112 }
400 -> message too large (default max 1 MB)
503 -> not enough in-sync replicas (NotEnoughReplicas)

Consumer

POST /v1/groups/billing/subscribe   { "topics": ["orders"] }

GET  /v1/groups/billing/poll?maxBytes=1048576&timeoutMs=500
200 { "records": [ {"topic":"orders","partition":3,"offset":889112,
                    "key":"user-42","value":"<b64>"} ] }

POST /v1/groups/billing/commit
{ "offsets": [ {"topic":"orders","partition":3,"offset":889113} ] }

Admin

POST /v1/topics   { "name":"orders", "partitions":24, "replicationFactor":3,
                    "config":{"retention.ms":604800000, "min.insync.replicas":2} }

Real Kafka uses a binary TCP protocol (Produce, Fetch, OffsetCommit, JoinGroup), but the semantics above are the same: producers pick the partition (by key hash), consumers pull and commit offsets.

Industry example. Kafka's acks=all + min.insync.replicas=2 is the standard "do not lose data" setting.

Everyday analogy. The producer drops a letter into numbered mailboxes; readers say "I have read up to letter 889,112".

Common interview traps.

  • A push-based consumer design that overwhelms slow consumers (Kafka pulls for backpressure).
  • Forgetting offsets belong to the consumer group.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 1M messages/s peak, 1 KB each, retention 7 days, replication factor 3.

Quantity Calculation Result
Ingress 1M x 1 KB 1 GB/s
Replication traffic x2 extra copies 2 GB/s between brokers
Egress (3 consumer groups) 3 x 1 GB/s 3 GB/s
Daily data 1 GB/s x 86,400 ~86 TB/day raw
7-day retention with RF 3 86 TB x 7 x 3 ~1.8 PB (a lot; usually average load is 10x lower)
Brokers (50 MB/s/disk-friendly, say 100 MB/s per broker write incl. replication) 3 GB/s total write / 0.1 ~30 brokers
Partitions per-partition throughput ~10 MB/s (conservative) 1 GB/s / 10 MB/s = 100 partitions min; choose 200 to 600

Use average (say 100k msg/s) for storage: 100 MB/s x 86,400 = 8.6 TB/day, x7 x3 = ~180 TB. Real design sizes disks for average, network for peak.

Partition count rule of thumb: target throughput / per-partition throughput, and at least the max number of consumers you want running in parallel in one group.

Everyday analogy. Estimating how many newspaper printing presses and warehouses you need, given edition size and how long you keep copies.

Common interview traps.

  • Sizing storage for peak instead of average.
  • Forgetting replication multiplies both disk and network.
  • Setting thousands of partitions per topic "to be safe" (costs memory, open files, election time).

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components

  • Broker: a server holding partition logs on disk.
  • Topic -> partitions: each partition is an ordered, append-only log; the unit of parallelism and ordering.
  • Replication: each partition has a leader and followers; followers copy the leader. Reads and writes go to the leader.
  • Controller / metadata quorum: elects leaders and tracks cluster state (ZooKeeper historically, KRaft in Kafka 3.x onward).
  • Consumer groups: each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer within a group; groups are independent.
  • Producers choose partition by hash(key) % partitions (same key goes to the same partition, preserving per-key order).

Decision gravity. Partition count is nearly a one-way door: you can increase it, but doing so changes hash(key) % n and breaks key-to-partition ordering for existing keys; decreasing it requires a new topic. Replication factor 3 is a deliberate cost for durability; RF=1 is reversible but loses data on a disk failure.

Industry examples. LinkedIn runs trillions of messages/day on Kafka; Uber built tiering and federation on top; Confluent, MSK and Redpanda offer managed or compatible versions. Pulsar separates compute (brokers) from storage (BookKeeper) as an alternative.

Everyday analogy. A post office with many numbered sorting lanes; each lane has one clerk (leader) and two backups.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a topic as a whole is ordered (only each partition is).
  • Having more consumers than partitions and expecting more parallelism (extras sit idle).

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Why a log is fast: sequential disk and zero copy

Each partition is a directory of segment files (for example 1 GB each) named by their first offset, plus an index (offset to file position). Writes only append, and sequential disk I/O is fast (hundreds of MB/s on HDD, GB/s on SSD). Kafka relies on the OS page cache instead of its own cache and uses sendfile (zero copy) to move bytes from page cache to the network without copying through user space.

partition-3/
  00000000000000000000.log     offsets 0 .. 889,000
  00000000000000000000.index   sparse offset -> byte position
  00000000000000889001.log     active segment (being appended)

Reading from an offset: binary search the segment list by name, then the sparse index, then scan a few KB. Messages are batched and compressed (lz4/zstd) per batch, giving 3x to 5x savings.

Replication, ISR and leader election

  • Followers fetch from the leader like consumers. The set of followers that are caught up is the ISR (in-sync replicas).
  • A message is committed once all ISR members have it; consumers only see committed messages (up to the high-water mark).
  • Producer acks: 0 (fire and forget), 1 (leader only, may lose on leader crash), all (every ISR member).
  • min.insync.replicas=2 with RF=3: if ISR shrinks below 2, writes fail rather than risk loss (safety over availability).
  • Leader dies: the controller picks a new leader from the ISR, so no committed message is lost. unclean.leader.election.enable=false prevents electing an out-of-sync replica (which would lose data).

Worked example. RF=3, acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2: can lose any 1 broker with no data loss and no downtime; losing 2 brokers stops writes to affected partitions but keeps committed data.

Decision gravity. acks=all costs ~1 extra network round trip (a few ms) for durability; reversible per producer. Allowing unclean election is a deliberate availability-over-consistency choice, risky to flip on later.

Consumer groups and rebalancing

Partitions are assigned among consumers in the group (range, round-robin, or cooperative sticky assignors). Each consumer tracks an offset per partition, committed to an internal topic __consumer_offsets.

When a consumer joins, leaves or misses heartbeats (session.timeout.ms=45000), the group rebalances: partitions are reassigned and, in the old "eager" protocol, all consumers pause. Cooperative rebalancing moves only affected partitions.

Production incident pattern. Symptom: consumer lag grows and stays high, processing pauses in waves. Metric: records-lag-max, rebalance count. Cause: slow processing exceeds max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 min), the broker thinks the consumer died and rebalances repeatedly. Fix: process less per poll (max.poll.records), or increase the interval, or move work to a thread pool.

Delivery semantics

Semantics How Risk
At most once Commit offset before processing Loses messages on crash
At least once Process, then commit Duplicates on crash/retry
Exactly once Idempotent producer + transactions + commit offsets in the same transaction Higher overhead, only within Kafka

Idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true): each producer has an ID, each message a sequence number per partition; the broker drops duplicates from retries. Transactions write to several partitions and the consumer offsets atomically (used by Kafka Streams). Across external systems (a DB), exactly once means at-least-once plus an idempotent consumer (dedupe by message ID or upsert).

Retention, compaction and ordering

  • Time/size retention: delete whole old segments (retention.ms=7 days, retention.bytes). Cheap: deleting a file.
  • Log compaction: keep only the latest value per key (for changelogs, such as a user profile table). Tombstone (null value) deletes a key.
  • Ordering: guaranteed within a partition. Use a key (for example orderId) so related events land together. Hot key (one huge customer) overloads one partition: add salting or sub-keys if order across them is not needed.
  • Poison messages: a message that always fails; send to a dead letter topic after N retries rather than blocking the partition.

Pull vs push, and backpressure

Consumers pull, so a slow consumer simply lags without overwhelming itself or the broker. Long polling (fetch.max.wait.ms) avoids empty round trips. Push systems (RabbitMQ default) need prefetch limits to avoid flooding.

Beyond one cluster

Cross-region: MirrorMaker 2 or Cluster Linking replicates topics asynchronously. Tiered storage (Kafka 3.6+, early access then production-maturing; confirm in docs) offloads old segments to S3 to cut disk cost.

Everyday analogy. The ISR is the group of backup clerks who have the same ledger as the head clerk; you only announce a letter as "received" when all the up-to-date backups have written it down.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming exactly-once delivery everywhere; it is only effectively-once with idempotent consumers outside Kafka.
  • Setting acks=1 and being surprised by data loss on leader failure.
  • Not mentioning consumer lag as the key health metric.
  • Adding consumers beyond the partition count.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• The log abstraction: partitions, offsets, retention, replay, consumer groups.
  • Numbers: throughput, partitions per topic, brokers, replication overhead, retention storage.
  • Replication: leader/follower, ISR, acks, min.insync.replicas, what is lost in each failure.
  • Ordering guarantees (per-partition) and key choice.
  • Delivery semantics and idempotency, with honest limits of exactly-once.
  • Operational thinking: lag monitoring, rebalances, poison messages, hot partitions.
  • Seniors compare Kafka with RabbitMQ/SQS/Pulsar, discuss KRaft replacing ZooKeeper, tiered storage, multi-region replication and schema evolution (Schema Registry, Avro/Protobuf).

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing boxes (broker, ZooKeeper) with no explanation of the log and replication.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Kafka-like = partitioned, replicated, append-only log with retention; consumers pull and track offsets.
  • Partition = unit of ordering and parallelism; key hash picks it; partition count is hard to change safely.
  • Speed comes from sequential I/O, batching, compression, page cache and zero-copy.
  • Durability: RF=3, acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2, no unclean election; committed data survives one broker loss.
  • Consumer groups share partitions; rebalances and lag are the main operational pain.
  • At-least-once plus idempotent consumers is the practical default; exactly-once needs idempotent producer and transactions.
  • The log-vs-queue choice and partition count are the near one-way doors.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between a Kafka-style log and a classic queue like RabbitMQ or SQS, and why does it matter for design?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the root decision; wrong answer means the rest of the design is off.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A log is append-only and retained; each consumer group keeps its own offset and can replay old messages, and many groups read the same data independently. A classic queue deletes a message after it is acked, supports per-message redelivery and often priorities, but you cannot replay. I pick a log when I need replay, fan-out to many consumers and high throughput; a queue when I need per-message ack, delays or priorities.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Log: partitions are ordered, immutable sequences; position is an offset; retention by time/size (for example 7 days).
  • Consumer pulls and commits its offset, so a slow consumer just lags; backpressure is built in.
  • Queue: broker tracks per-message state (in flight, acked, DLQ); push with prefetch limits.
  • Ordering: only within a partition in a log.
Producer -> Topic partition (log) -> Consumer group A (offset 889112)
                                  -> Consumer group B (offset 120)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating Kafka like RabbitMQ: expecting per-message delete or priorities.
  • Thinking a topic as a whole is ordered.
  • Forgetting offsets belong to the consumer group.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a log do retries per message? -> Not natively; use retry topics or a DLQ.
  2. Why pull rather than push? -> Backpressure; consumers control rate.
  3. Migration cost between them? -> High: consumers depend on offset semantics.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists features. The senior frames it by access pattern (replay, fan-out, throughput) and states the decision is costly to reverse.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team used a log for a job queue and had no per-job retry or priority; a poison message stalled a partition until they added a dead letter topic.

questions.promptHtml: Explain acks, ISR and min.insync.replicas. What settings give you "no committed message is lost when one broker dies"?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Core durability mechanics; many engineers set acks=all and think they are done.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each partition has a leader and followers; the ISR is the set of followers caught up with the leader. A message is committed once all ISR members have it. With RF=3, acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2 and unclean leader election disabled, any single broker can die with no loss of committed data and no downtime; if two die, writes stop (safety over availability) but committed data remains.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• acks=0 fire and forget; acks=1 leader only (lost if leader crashes before followers copy); acks=all all ISR members.
  • min.insync.replicas=2: if ISR shrinks below 2, producers get NotEnoughReplicas rather than risking loss.
  • Leader dies: the controller elects a new leader from the ISR, which has all committed messages.
  • unclean.leader.election.enable=false stops an out-of-sync replica becoming leader (which would lose data).
  • Cost of acks=all: about one extra network round trip (a few ms); reversible per producer.
Producer -> Leader -> Follower 1
                  -> Follower 2    ack when all ISR have it

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• acks=all with min.insync.replicas=1: with ISR of one, it is effectively acks=1.
  • Leaving unclean election on.
  • Assuming exactly-once because acks=all.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What shrinks the ISR? -> A follower falling behind or dying (replica lag time exceeded).
  2. Why not RF=2? -> One failure leaves no margin: min.insync=2 would block writes.
  3. When allow unclean election? -> Only when availability matters more than losing a few messages (metrics, logs).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "acks=all is safe". Senior: needs min.insync.replicas, RF, unclean election and states what each failure costs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cluster with acks=1 lost a few seconds of orders when a leader crashed during deploy.

questions.contextHtml: Peak 1M messages/s, 1 KB each, average load is 100k msg/s, retention 7 days, RF=3, three consumer groups read everything. Brokers handle about 100 MB/s write each including replication (conservative).
questions.promptHtml: Size brokers, partitions and storage. State what you size for peak vs average.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Sizes storage for peak (1.8 PB) and ignores network.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Compression? Is the average-to-peak ratio stable? Is tiered storage allowed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Network is the peak constraint; disk is sized by average; partitions by throughput and consumer parallelism.
  4. How I'd verify each: Ingress 1 GB/s; replication 2 extra copies = 2 GB/s inter-broker; egress 3 x 1 GB/s = 3 GB/s. Write load across the cluster: 3 GB/s / 0.1 = about 30 brokers. Storage on average: 100 MB/s x 86,400 = 8.6 TB/day, x7 x3 = about 180 TB (peak sizing would be about 1.8 PB). Partitions: at about 10 MB/s each, 1 GB/s / 10 = 100 minimum; choose 200 to 600, at least as many as the max consumers per group.
  5. Root cause: N/A.
  6. Fix: About 30 brokers, topics at 200 to 600 partitions, retention disks about 180 TB plus headroom (compression 3x to 5x lowers it), network sized for peak.
  7. Prevention: Alerts on disk, under-replicated partitions and network saturation.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not create thousands of partitions "to be safe": memory, open files and election time grow with partitions.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Retention 30 days? -> Tiered storage to S3 to cut disk cost.
  • Add consumers beyond partitions? -> Extras idle.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A topic with 5,000 partitions made controller failover take minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: forgets replication.
  • Hire: correct network and storage maths.
  • Strong hire: peak vs average distinction and partition sizing rationale.

questions.contextHtml:
Order-processing consumers in group billing show lag climbing and processing pausing in waves every few minutes.

records-lag-max: 2.1M (was ~5k)
rebalance count last hour: 38
consumer log: "Member ... sending LeaveGroup request ... consumer poll timeout has expired"
max.poll.interval.ms=300000  max.poll.records=500
avg processing per record: 1.4 s after a new fraud-check API call was added

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds more consumers or partitions immediately.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed? Is the lag on all partitions? Is the downstream API slow?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Lower max.poll.records (for example 50) so a batch finishes inside the interval; scale the downstream call if throttled.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Processing of one batch exceeds max.poll.interval.ms (500 x 1.4 s = 700 s > 300 s); GC; broker-side issues.
  4. How I'd verify each: The consumer log message, batch durations, rebalance metrics.
  5. Root cause: The broker thinks the consumer is dead after the poll interval expires; rebalances pause the group, and the same slow batch repeats after reassignment, causing a loop.
  6. Fix: Reduce records per poll, move slow work to a worker pool while keeping polling (pausing partitions as needed), cooperative sticky assignor to avoid stop-the-world, static membership for rolling restarts.
  7. Prevention: Alert on rebalance rate and lag; load test with slow downstream.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just raise max.poll.interval.ms to hours: failure detection becomes slow. Adding consumers does not help if the loop is rebalancing.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Duplicates after rebalance? -> At-least-once: dedupe by message id or idempotent writes.
  • Poison message? -> Dead letter topic after N retries.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A new synchronous call in a consumer made each batch slower than the poll interval; the group rebalanced forever.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: add consumers.
  • Hire: ties to poll interval and batch size.
  • Strong hire: cooperative rebalancing, worker pools with pause, DLQ.

questions.contextHtml: Topic orders has 24 partitions keyed by customerId. One enterprise customer generates 35% of traffic. That partition's broker is at 90% disk throughput and the consumer for it lags by 40 minutes while 23 others are idle. Business requires order of events per order, not per customer.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Increases partitions to 48.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is ordering truly needed per order only? Can the consumer process in parallel within the partition?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add consumer-side parallelism for that partition keyed by orderId; throttle the customer's producer if needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Bad key choice (customer is too coarse); partition count is irrelevant for one key.
  4. How I'd verify each: Bytes per partition, key distribution, per-partition lag.
  5. Root cause: All events of one key go to one partition; more partitions do not split one key.
  6. Fix: Key by orderId (ordering per order is enough); or salt the key (customerId#0..7) if only coarse ordering is needed.
  7. Prevention: Key distribution checks in design review; alerts on partition skew.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Adding partitions changes hash(key) % n and breaks key-to-partition ordering for existing keys during the transition; reducing partitions needs a new topic.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Migrate existing keys? -> New topic with new key, dual-publish, switch consumers by offset.
  • Order across salts? -> Lost; accept or merge by timestamp downstream.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single tenant key saturated one partition for hours until the key changed to the order id.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds partitions.
  • Hire: re-keys by finer entity.
  • Strong hire: understands ordering needs and migration impact.

questions.contextHtml: A payment service consumes payment-requests and writes to Postgres and a bank API. The product manager says: "we need exactly-once". During a broker leader change last week, 312 requests were processed twice and 41 customers were charged twice.
questions.promptHtml: What do you promise and what do you build?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Enable exactly-once in Kafka and it is solved."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which side effects are external (DB, bank)? Does the bank API accept an idempotency key? What is the cost of a missed vs duplicate charge?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add dedupe by request id before charging; refund duplicates.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: At-least-once delivery after producer retry or consumer crash before offset commit.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare message ids and offsets in the processed logs; check producer idempotence config; look at commit timing.
  5. Root cause: Process-then-commit gives at-least-once; a crash or rebalance between the charge and the commit redelivers the message.
  6. Fix: Idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true); consumer uses a unique request id as an idempotency key in the bank call and a unique constraint in the DB (upsert), so processing twice has the effect of once. Kafka transactions give exactly-once only for Kafka-to-Kafka flows (consume, process, produce plus offsets in one transaction).
  7. Prevention: Duplicate-rate metric; a replay test with forced redelivery.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not promise exactly-once delivery; I promise effectively-once through idempotency. At-most-once would lose payments.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Bank API without idempotency keys? -> Record intent in DB first (outbox), then call; reconcile on timeouts.
  • Overhead of transactions? -> Higher latency, only within Kafka.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Double charges after a rebalance were fixed by an idempotency key on the payment call, not by Kafka settings.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "exactly-once flag".
  • Hire: at-least-once plus idempotent consumer.
  • Strong hire: outbox, reconciliation, clarity on scope of Kafka transactions.

questions.contextHtml:
RF=3, acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2. Broker 4 and broker 7 (both in rack B) go down at 03:10. Alerts:

UnderReplicatedPartitions: 112
OfflinePartitionsCount: 0
producer errors: NotEnoughReplicasException on 31 partitions
producer errors: none on the rest

Some partitions had both followers on brokers 4 and 7.
questions.promptHtml: What happens, and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Enable unclean leader election to restore writes."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can I recover the brokers quickly? Are those partitions critical? Is data loss acceptable for any topic?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Bring brokers back; if impossible, reassign replicas for affected partitions to healthy brokers. Let producers buffer and retry.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Partitions whose ISR dropped below 2 reject writes by design; replica placement not rack-aware.
  4. How I'd verify each: kafka-topics --describe --under-min-isr-partitions, controller logs, replica placement.
  5. Root cause: ISR shrank to 1 for those partitions; min.insync.replicas=2 correctly blocks writes. Both followers sat in the same failure domain.
  6. Fix: Restore brokers (they catch up and rejoin ISR); throttled partition reassignment to move replicas; rack-aware placement (broker.rack).
  7. Prevention: Rack awareness, alerts on under-min-ISR, capacity so a rack loss does not overload survivors.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not enable unclean election to resume writes: it risks silently losing committed messages. This is an explicit availability vs durability choice, made earlier.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Leader dies with acks=1? -> Messages only on that leader are lost.
  • Reassignment traffic? -> Throttle to protect live traffic.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rack outage showed that replicas had been placed unevenly after years of manual reassignments.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: unclean election.
  • Hire: ISR reasoning, restore brokers.
  • Strong hire: rack awareness, throttled reassignment, trade-off framing.

questions.subtopic: Partition count change under live traffic
questions.contextHtml: Topic clicks has 12 partitions, 40 MB/s, consumers cannot keep up and you need 48 parallel consumers. Messages are keyed by sessionId and downstream aggregation depends on per-session order. You cannot lose data or order, and cannot have downtime.
questions.promptHtml: How do you go from 12 to 48 partitions?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Just alter the topic to 48."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is strict per-session order required across the transition? How long can consumers tolerate lag? Can I dual-run?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Scale consumers within current limits (12) and optimise processing; stay stable.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Changing the partition count changes hash(key) % n, so a session can land on a different partition mid-flight, breaking order.
  4. How I'd verify each: Test key-to-partition mapping before and after; check consumer assumptions.
  5. Root cause: Key-partition mapping is tied to partition count.
  6. Fix: Create clicks-v2 with 48 partitions; producers dual-write (or a mirror job copies); consumers of v1 drain to a cut-over offset; start v2 consumers at the matching point; switch producers; retire v1 after retention. If per-session order matters only inside a session window, cut over at a quiet boundary.
  7. Prevention: Choose partitions with growth headroom (rule: target throughput / per-partition throughput, plus max consumers); document the one-way door.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not alter in place with strict ordering requirements; it is cheap but breaks guarantees. Over-partitioning costs memory, files and election time.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Compacted topic? -> Same new-topic approach; replay the log into the new topic.
  • Consumers stuck on partitions that are quiet? -> Cooperative rebalancing and monitoring per partition.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An in-place partition increase broke session ordering for an hour and produced corrupted aggregates that took a day to recompute.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: alters in place without thought.
  • Hire: new topic with migration.
  • Strong hire: dual-write, cut-over, ordering analysis and prevention.
